text: Good afternoon. I call to order the September 10th, 2026 Loudoun County School Board and Loudoun County Board of Supervisors joint committee meeting. Welcome everyone to the LCPS boardroom. We're happy to host the joint committee this afternoon, and we'll start today with public comments. I understand that we have two public speakers today. Thank you for engaging with the joint committee through the public comment process.

We welcome comments from Loudoun County residents and believe that strong community engagement and outreach are important components of a successful school system. Speakers must limit comments to the time allotted. Based on the number of speakers and the agenda this evening, all speakers have been allotted two minutes each for public comment. Please be advised that speakers who miss their time slot will not be called at a later time. All audience members shall maintain civility, decorum, and respect for the functioning and dignity of the joint committee at all times.

Please remain seated unless arriving, departing, speaking at the podium, or during a break. Shouting, heckling, jeering, applause, and other noise which disrupts or delays the meeting, these are considered violations of civility, decorum, and respect. Obstructing speakers from being able to see the school board and vice versa, interrupting speakers, attempting to speak when not called to do so by the chair, and approaching a speaker- Who are otherwise attempting to intimidate, disparage, or distract a speaker, staff member, or other meeting attendees.

Speakers should refrain from vulgarity, obscenities, defamation, profanity, and other like breaches of respect, nor may speakers target, criticize, or attack individual students and/or individual division employees during public comment. As a reminder, school board Policy 2520 states, "Speakers may not target, criticize, or attack individual students during public comment. Speakers should communicate those concerns to their school principal or an appropriate school official. The school board requests that comments on an

individual student or employee-related matter not be shared at public meetings where the disclosure could violate applicable confidentiality requirements." Speakers should direct their comments toward the committee. And please understand that the committee will not respond in any way directly to the public during the public comment period.

Violations of decorum and civility by any meeting attendee may result in the chair directing staff to remove the attendee from the remainder of the meeting. Repeated or persistent violations of decorum, civility by the audience may result in on the decision of the chair, public comment being tabled to a later time in the meeting, limiting the number of attendees in the meeting room, or public comment ending for the evening. We do look forward to hearing your comments.

Our first speaker today is Madeline Marlowe, and the next speaker is Susan Jones. Oh, we have online public comment today? Sure. Yep. Is there a speaker here, Ms. Marlowe? Yes, this is Madeline Marlowe. Great. The floor is yours. Excellent. Thank you so much for having me here today.

I'm here today to express my gratitude and also express urgency for the action item regarding the expansion of the Safe Passages to Schools program. I'm a lifelong Virginia resident. I lived in Loudoun County for 10 years now, and I am a parent. My son is zoned to attend Newton Lee Elementary School in two years. I am so grateful that there is moving forward, and attention, and resources being

dedicated to the Safe Passages to Schools or Safe Routes to Schools program. I really wanted to come before the board to urge a comprehensive and holistic approach. Supervisor Turner and his staff might recognize my name from the, hopefully, polite nagging emails about the Crosswalk Request program that I heard about for Loudoun County in a separate context. I was delighted to see that that was included in the meeting materials for today.

I urge the board, both the board of supervisors and the school board, to take a comprehensive, holistic approach for this, not just for the probably minority of students who will walk to school for 180 days per year, but for the entire community that will use pedestrian infrastructure for 365 days per year. A street that works for an eight-year-old works for an 80-year-old, and I am completely fine with Safe Passages to School being the way that we target and

prioritize the investment in our community. But this is not just for the literal, actual students of the school during the school year. It is increasing pedestrian dignity and safety for the entire county. So thank you so much, and please consider holistically and comprehensively how this really will benefit everyone. I appreciate your time and your hard work. Thank you. Our in-person speaker is Susan Jones.

Hello. My name is Susan Jones. I'm in the Broad Run District, and I met with Sylvia Glass and Ross Svendsen to talk about a Loudoun County Citizens Academy. I was born and raised in Virginia, grew up and went through the Fairfax County Public Schools, graduated from Virginia Tech, grew up with a mother who listened to WTOP every waking moment of every

day. And yet, I grew up not knowing about Virginia state and local government. In fact, the first time I ever went to the Capitol is when my husband and I decided to visit all 50 state capitals, and so we went to Richmond in 2019. And just this year, I found out about the Dillon Rule. So I do not think that I am the only person in Loudoun

County that doesn't have a good appreciation of state and local government. After all, many people move into this area all the time. So I did some research on other public academies. I researched Blacksburg, Virginia, Montgomery County, Virginia, which has partnered with Christiansburg, and the city of Alexandria. All of those have citizens academies.

They're run by their office of public relations or public affairs, and they're eight to 10 weeks long. They involve visits to government facilities. They include things like mock budget or mock board of supervisor meetings. And they end up creating a lot of interest in local government. In fact, some of the participants in these programs have gone on to run for public office and/or

participate in the various committees that you have. Thank you so much for your public comment. We want to thank all of our participants for coming out today and for providing your thoughtful comments. That will conclude the public comment session for today. And we will now move on to the co-chair's report on the joint committee, and this will cover board of supervisor and school board activities.

Typically, as the acting chair for this evening, I'll start, and then I will pass the mic over to my co-chair, Glass. Good evening, joint committee members, and to our families and communities watching at home. We are off to a wonderful start to the school year across Loudoun County Public Schools, with students, staff, and community partners continuing to demonstrate growth, leadership, and a commitment to belonging and opportunity for

all. Reports released by the Virginia Department of Education on August 25th show continued strong improvement by LCPS students as measured by the 2026 Standards of Learning tests. The results indicate that SOL proficiency rates have increased or remain the same in most subject areas. LCPS students demonstrate strong performance, consistently outpacing statewide averages across all five subject areas.

In English, reading, mathematics, and science, LCPS achieved a pass rate of plus nine percentage points higher than the Virginia state averages. In English writing, LCPS achieved an 89% pass rate compared to the state average of 76%, a difference of 13 percentage points. In history and social studies, LCPS achieved an 88% pass rate compared to

the state average of 70%, a difference of 18 percentage points. These results reflect the positive impact of school support systems, division initiatives, the work of our educators, and strong partnerships with our families. Honoring staff leadership and opportunity. Six LCPS middle schools, Belmont Ridge Middle School, Blue Ridge Middle School, Eagle Ridge Middle School, Riverbend Middle School, Smartts Mill Middle School, and

Watson Mountain Middle School, have been recognized as 2026 Schools of Distinction by the Association of Middle Level Education. This is the second time Belmont Ridge, Riverbend, and Smartts Mill have received this recognition. These six LCPS schools are among just 39 middle schools and the only Virginia middle schools recognized by the AMLE for their commitment to young adolescent education and continuous improvement.

These schools set the standard for best practices for middle grades. Through a rigorous evaluation process, Schools of Distinction demonstrate excellence in implementing best practices and continuous improvement plans supported by stakeholder interviews with staff, students, and families. The LCPS schools honored this year joined seven other LCPS middle schools,

Brambleton, Farmwell Station, Gum Spring, J. Michael Lunsford, Seneca Ridge, J. Lumpkin Simpson, and Willard Middle School, recognized previously as Schools of Distinction Building community and belonging. LCPS and HealthWorks for Northern Virginia are partnering to bring medical, dental, and mental healthcare services directly to students, families, and staff through two new mobile health clinics. These specially outfitted buses, which arrived on

Thursday, August 27th, mark an important step towards expanding access to care across the community. By delivering healthcare where it is needed most, this partnership helps individuals and families access essential services. Healthcare access plays a critical role in overall wellbeing and can directly affect a student's ability to attend school consistently and succeed in the

classroom. To celebrate the launch of the mobile clinics and this innovative partnership, LCPS and HealthWorks will host a ribbon-cutting ceremony and open house this fall. Following the ribbon-cutting ceremony, the mobile clinics will provide services at three pilot locations, Sully Elementary School, Sterling Middle School, and Park View High School, before expanding to additional LCPS schools next year. Thank you, and that concludes my report.

Co-Chair Glass, would you like to present your report? Yes, and thank you, Co-Chair Chandler. I would like to welcome back students, families, staff, and faculty as we begin another academic school year. I wish us a safe and successful year ahead. This year, I'm back at our school at Sanders Corner, and it was great to see Dr. Spence come and visit there

last week. It's always great to see folks come in and see what a great job our schools are doing. I'm so thankful for our school community, and it will have a great year. On behalf of the Board of Supervisors, I thank you for your continued invitations. winning the 2026 Virginia High School League State Championship. At the July meeting, the Freedom High School boys tennis team and the boys track and field team were honored for winning the 2026 Virginia High School League Class 5 State Championship. The CIF estimates how much money a new home will cost the county in terms of building things like schools, parks, and other public facilities. Through proffers, developers may pay the county those CIFs to offset the burden on services for the new homes. This adjustment was made because LCPS shared that they are unlikely to need any new school buildings for the next 10 years.

At the board's public hearing next week, we are slated to approve legislative land use applications that will allow for the construction of a joint central Loudoun Services and storage center off Sicklerville Road in Leesburg for both the county government and LCPS, along with the approvals to renovate and expand Waterford Elementary School. The board looks forward to continuing working with

LCPS and the school board to best serve our residents. That is my co-chair report. Thank you. Thank you, Co-Chair Glass. With that, we'll move on to item number four, information items. First up, item 4.01, the use of publicly owned property for attainable housing. This will be presented this evening by Travis Perlman and Eric Keeler, Housing and Community Development, Jefferson Miller and Adnan Mamoon, Support Services from LCPS. Madam Chair.

Thank you for that clarification.

Looks like we're ready to begin. Gentlemen, please, the floor is yours. Well, thank you. My name is Eric Keeler. I'm the Director of Housing & Community Development here in the county, and I'm joined by Travis Perlman, and he's going to take us through this presentation. It was presented to our Transportation and Land Use Committee, and now we would like to share it with you. It's just an analysis of publicly owned land that includes both county and school-owned land. So I'll hand it over to Travis.

Thank you so much, Director Keeler. Good afternoon, committee chair, co-chair, and committee members. As Director Keeler said, my name's Travis Perlman with the Loudoun County Housing Department. Tonight, I'll be providing an update on the use of publicly owned property for the development of attainable and workforce housing. Next slide, please. So specifically, tonight I'll be discussing the policy justification for using

publicly owned property to develop attainable and workforce housing, as well as analyses that have been recently completed and are currently ongoing to support the advancement of county and Loudoun County Public School-owned property for this activity. Next slide, please. The county's Unmet Housing Needs Strategic Plan adopted in 2021 identifies the use of public land and facilities for housing as one of 26 planned strategies. Three key benefits of leveraging public property for attainable and workforce

housing include reducing the local subsidy necessary to finance and support the development of housing, facilitating more intentional development reflective of community and policy priorities, and retaining the ability to maintain long-term ownership of property to drive future redevelopment plans and ensure ongoing affordability. In fall 2024, staff from the county's Department of Housing & Community Development, Office of Real Property Asset Management Planning, and County

Administration convened with staff from Loudoun County Public Schools' Department of Support Services and kicked off a joint working group to evaluate the use of county and school-owned property for the development of attainable and workforce housing. Next slide, please. An initial outcome of this working group has been the completion of a property suitability analysis and the publication of a public-facing ArcGIS dashboard

reflecting results of this analysis. The dashboard is currently published on the county's GeoHub website and was presented to the Transportation and Land Use Committee of the county at their January 2026 committee meeting. The objectives of the property suitability analysis were to develop a shared methodology for analyzing public property for the suitability of attainable and workforce housing, develop an informational resource to share the results of the analysis, present and obtain feedback from policymakers

on the results of the analysis, including key characteristics of properties that should be considered for the development of attainable and workforce housing, and to propose next steps on how to operationalize the results of the analysis and continue to advance the use of publicly owned property for this activity. Staff did their best to apply a standardized and objective methodology for analyzing publicly owned property for the development of attainable housing that

evaluated whether a parcel of property could physically be developed with housing, irrespective of its existing place, type, and zoning. Staff classified the development suitability of parcels into three categories, including not suitable, potentially suitable, and suitable. Parcels identified as not suitable cannot be physically developed with housing and are either fully encumbered by an environmental feature such as floodplain,

encumbered by a conservation easement, or located within the 65-plus LDN Airport Overlay District. Parcels identified as potentially suitable could potentially be physically developed with housing. However, most of these properties are either developed with an existing use or planned for future development with a non-residential use. Attainable housing on these parcels would either need to be co-located with an existing county or school facility, or a planned capital project would need to be

modified to incorporate housing as a future use. Also included in this category are parcels entirely developed with an existing use that would require the redevelopment of the existing facility in order to add housing to the property. Parcels identified as suitable are those parcels that are not fully encumbered by features that would prevent them from being developed with housing and have no existing or planned use.

I will add that Loudoun County Public Schools applied a slightly narrower criteria than the county did and classified those school-owned parcels that are fully developed with a school use as not suitable. The classification of each county and school-owned parcel is summarized on the table on this slide. The county and Loudoun County Public Schools own 256 and 114 parcels of property each, totaling approximately 5,248 and

3,214 acres respectively. Approximately 46% of the parcels are classified as not suitable, with the remaining 54% being classified as potentially suitable. No county or school-owned parcel was identified as suitable, and this is because given that the county and LCPS may only acquire land for an authorized public

purpose, all land that is either owned or recently acquired is either improved in addressing a specific use or is planned for the development of a future non-residential use. Next slide, please. As mentioned previously, county staff have included the results of the analysis in an ArcGIS dashboard that is publicly available on the county's GeoHub website under the name Property Suitability Analysis.

The dashboard identifies the suitability classification and development opportunity of each parcel, allows the user to filter parcels by suitability classification, county election district, and owner. It includes relevant data about each parcel, such as parcel size, policy area, place type, zoning, existing or planned use, and potential development limitations. Users also have the ability to turn on and off more than 20 other GIS layers

related to land use, environmental features, and transportation for additional analysis. County and LCPS staff are continuing to consider feedback from the Transportation and Land Use Committee meeting from January on how to use this property suitability analysis and operationalize it to continue to advance the use of publicly owned land for this activity.

An item will be presented at next week's Board of Supervisors meeting, that is being sponsored by the Department of Transportation and Capital Infrastructure and supported by the Department of Housing and Community Development, requesting conceptual approval from the Board of Supervisors to consider development of attainable housing on a existing county-owned property. Additionally, county LCPS Attainable and Workforce Housing Working Group is conducting an additional comparative analysis on the implications of different

ownership and project management delivery models for attainable and workforce housing on LCPS-owned property. The analysis and response to the new authority granted to school entities to retain ownership of land on which workforce housing is developed through the passage of House Bill 1130 in the Commonwealth's General Assembly this last legislative session. The working group anticipates discussing the results of this analysis with county

and LCPS leadership in the coming months and to request additional direction on how to continue to advance the use of LCPS-owned property for attainable or workforce housing. This concludes staff presentation, and we're available for any questions or feedback that you may have. Thank you, gentlemen, for the presentation. Thank you for being here this evening. Keeler, for this informative presentation. You might have already answered my question, but just in case, I just need a clarification. I noticed that it was zero parcels that were identified as immediately suitable in that table that you showed. As I mentioned, most of these properties are either planned for a future capital project, and so those project scopes would need to be modified to incorporate attainable housing, which would require affirmative direction and action from the board, or there's an existing use on the property, and there may be some vacant land where attainable housing could be co-located next

to an existing facility. But again, direction would need to be given to staff from the respective boards in order to move forward with that work. Supervisor Shaconi. Is that on? Okay, thank you, Vice Chair Chandler. So, you mentioned a narrow criteria that the schools are using regarding co-location. Can you explain that, please? Yeah. So I'm certainly not an expert on

state legislation as it relates to school entities. But as I understand, there are state statutes, or there is a state statute that speaks to certain requirements that have to be on a property for a school. And so where LCPS identified basically properties where there was no additional space because there was either they needed to meet one of those requirements or they were already meeting those requirements, and then those were

not considered suitable, or they were considered not suitable ultimately, because ultimately the school or one of the facilities that are required by state statute would need to be redeveloped. Okay, because I've always thought Tuscarora High School is a good pilot because there's a lot of land at that school that I thought could be

potentially co-located with affordable housing or attainable housing. Would HB 1130 help with this at all? So relating specifically to Tuscarora, I think that does fall into the potentially suitable category, and so again, given policy direction from respective boards, a project could be developed there physically.

1130 does create the opportunity for a school entity to retain ownership of land and have it developed as workforce housing specifically to serve employees. As I mentioned in the next steps, us as well as staff from the Department of Support Services with LCPS are conducting comparative analysis of the best way to move forward with the development of workforce housing or attainable housing on LCPS property, whether

the property should be conveyed to the county, whether the school entity retains ownership, who leads the project management aspect of that, and the implications of that under House Bill 1130, for instance. Yeah, and I think the housing authority that we're going to be discussing soon, I know you guys are bringing that back, I think has relevance here with HB 1130 in my view. But you don't need to answer that. That's coming to the board. So I've been an advocate of the housing authority. So I think this speaks to land banking.

I think the county is working on a policy for land banking, and I would like to see us start land banking maybe next to schools, school property because there is a real need for workforce housing for teachers and staff. So I think that's something to consider. And then I also would like to see a preference in some of our housing for

teachers and staff. I know we're not allowed to prioritize because of housing discrimination laws, but I think we've talked about this before. I brought this up at TLOC about a preference, not a priority. So I think, is that maybe something we could look into for some of our other projects besides the one from HB 1130? Sure. We can always work with the county attorney's office to see what the

legalities might be in adding that to some of our- Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Fine. Sorry. You had one more? I'm so excited about this, and I think it's such an innovative approach for us to take as a county, and I definitely embrace it.

I think one of the concerns that we work on all the time as a school board is a concern about declining enrollment, and one of the things that I see specific to the district that I represent is that the cost of housing is often an impediment. And the way it's changed in the 20 years that our family has lived here is really striking. Whereas when we moved into the community, our street was full of children, and you could literally open the door and toss your kids out, and there

was somebody to play with. And currently on the street I live on now, there's only one family that has elementary-aged children. I'm Algonquin District. The cost of housing is extremely high. I would imagine the average cost for a townhouse is close to six, and a single-family home is probably $850,000. So any thing that we can do, I think would be

beneficial to our entire community. That said, I am curious technically about one-- I'd love to know what it means. I love the dashboard, and I was digging around in it this afternoon. But, what does it mean, not fully encumbered by environmental features? So it means that part of the property... So when we're talking about environmental features, just for example, floodplain is

a big one. So fully encumbered means the entire property is covered by floodplain, so it cannot be physically developed. Not fully encumbered means at least a portion of the property is not covered by floodplain, and that portion of the property could be developed. Okay. And so if I heard you correctly for Dr. Rashid's question, the only reason why the graph shows zero is because we haven't changed our policies yet?

The only reason the graph shows zero is because, well, one, that was the classification that we decided to use. And to your point, affirmative policy action would need to be taken ultimately to move those properties from a potentially suitable category to a suitable category. Thank you for that. And then is there anyone on LCPS staff who could speak to

the reasons why the LCPS criteria is narrower around the school use issue? Yeah, I think Mr. Miller can speak to that. Good afternoon, everyone. Jefferson Miller, land management supervisor with LCPS. All of our sites, as you know, are identified as either an active school or a future school. And so much of the properties are utilized by that school program,

including their outdoor needs recreational space. So to, I think Mr. Kearney's question, if there's an outdoor sports field or walking track that meet the requirements of the school, we're not looking at the opportunity of redeveloping those. As Travis said, that would be needed a board action to move those forward. And there are probably other contributing factors around school property, including perhaps laws about how close to certain categories of citizens can be to school

property that could be potentially cumbersome around opening up housing on school sites to the general population as opposed to the workforce. Is that one of the distinctions why we would focus school property on workforce? I'm going to answer it slightly differently, and that sort of speaks to the comparative analysis on the property ownership portion. And so essentially, there's three options. Does the school board wish to retain property ownership and have the county be a major partner in running the project? All right. Well, thank you. The way that you answered it was very helpful. So I'll add a layer to all of this. There's financial tools that need to be used in order to finance. That it's not just county dollars.

We typically tie into federal, state, and all the other different layers that create the capital stack to build attainable housing or workforce housing. So those do come with other rules and regulations, which is getting to Supervisor Tecrobie's question before and one of the reasons why there are components that we have to look at. The only way to truly do everything would be for the county to upfront, put general

fund dollars to completely run the project. But at this point, we are leveraging one to three, four times the amount of county dollars going in with other funding sources in order to build and to make it affordable, the project truly affordable. So that is a component that we always have to consider. Thank you. Co-Chair Glass? Yes. I have a question.

With your list of the potentially suitable list from the LCPS side, does that include older schools or schools that are no longer being used? school board. It also includes proffered sites that have yet to be built on but would need further action by the board to identify. This review was really a desktop overview review of possibilities. Okay. And the other question, I think you kind of answered it.

drive many minutes, hours during the week to get to the school. Is there a way that we could maybe do a percentage of educators and staff to be in the workforce housing, or is that something that our laws say that's something we can't do? So it is one of the unique pieces of the new build that allows the school to

actually develop. So before this happened, the majority of the work was our office working and providing technical and that, and then the thought process was to transfer that property to the county because then we could dispose of it or ground lease it or do whatever was the direction of the board. Like I mentioned before, I think it comes back to how we build it and what type of

piece. If we do a mixed type of product, then there is a possibility where if we could not be leveraging funds, then we might be able to stay away from some of those preferences and the pieces. So we aren't having those general discussions and trying our office providing that technical assistance to the schools as to how do you actually build attainable housing, workforce housing. They're experts on the school side. So that's the continued joint component and discussions of who retains ownership, and what are the components. Okay. This sounds very exciting. Thank you.

Program, and over the past several years, the term Safe Routes to School and Safe Passages to School terms have been used interchangeably. However, they refer to the same program. any of the other county programs. The project team will work with partner agencies throughout the project. list will also be generated as a result of the analysis. So committee members, that concludes this presentation, and we are happy to answer or address any questions that you may have. All right.
